summary: Oak Bluffs bluff light at the approach to Vineyard Haven Harbor: a private light burned in 1871, the cast-iron tower of the 1870s stands today, a museum tends it.

structures.note: Cast-iron Italianate tower; the nomination dates it to 1876, LighthouseFriends to mid-1877 under construction

access.note: The Martha's Vineyard Museum keeps the doors open during visiting hours, with a keeper present. Adults $5, children 12 and under free. Sunday sunset openings from mid-June. Parking is limited on East Chop Drive; a VTA bus stops on East Chop Drive and New York Avenue, then a walk uphill.

facts.agency: Martha's Vineyard Museum (steward since 1994); the Archive lists the Museum as owner/manager, the 1981 nomination lists the Coast Guard as owner

events.note: Semaphore station at East Chop established to display shipping information (LighthouseFriends; Museum gives the early 1800s for the semaphore system)
Private light built by Captain Silas Daggett and maintained by subscriptions; the nomination says a wooden structure built at a cost of $1700
Private light destroyed by fire on Saturday 16 December 1871; keeper Capt. Luce and his daughter burned; no insurance. The nomination dates the fire to 1869
Light relit on 2 May 1872 with three Board-loaned reflectors atop Daggett's house, about 76 feet above the sea (LighthouseFriends)
Government purchase of the property, 1875 (nomination; Museum); LighthouseFriends gives 1876. Congress appropriated $5,000 for a light, reported February 1875
Cast-iron Italianate tower constructed (nomination); LighthouseFriends says a dwelling and cast-iron tower were under construction by mid-1877
US Lighthouse Society record: tower established 1877
Storm porch put over the tower door, and minor repairs
Oil house built for the kerosene used in the lantern
Changed from fixed white to flashing red (LighthouseFriends)
Illuminant changed from oil to electric incandescent
Keepers in the second and third districts, East Chop among them, sent data on the eclipse of the sun of 24 January 1925
Year automated, per the US Lighthouse Society record
Daymark returned from reddish-brown to white (LighthouseFriends)

corrections.why: 1869 was Daggett's private wooden light, burned in 1871. The cast-iron tower standing today is dated to 1876 (nomination) or 1877 (USLHS; LighthouseFriends has it under construction in mid-1877).
The USLHS record gives the tower as 40 feet, and LighthouseFriends calls it forty feet tall (12.2 m).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination's 1869 date for the fire is contradicted by two newspapers of December 1871 (New-York Herald 19 Dec; Worcester Daily Spy 21 Dec), which date a Saturday fire to 16 December 1871; the Museum and LighthouseFriends agree on 1871.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) fire year: nomination 1869 against the Herald and Spy of December 1871 (resolved toward 1871 in the story; the record's 1869 build date is the private light, which did burn in 1871); (2) government purchase: 1875 (nomination, Museum) against 1876 (LighthouseFriends); the $5,000 appropriation is reported in February 1875; (3) tower construction: nomination 1876, LighthouseFriends mid-1877 under construction, USLHS tower established 1877; the record's first-lit 1878 (Rowlett) is not checked against a source read here; (4) characteristic: the nomination (1981) gives an equal-interval group flashing 6-second light with a 300 mm lens and 9-mile range; LighthouseFriends gives fixed white until 1898, flashing red, then flashing green in 1934; the record's Iso G 6s is not supported by any source read here and is not in the facts; (5) owner: the 1981 nomination says Coast Guard; the USLHS record says the Museum; the Museum says steward; current title not settled; (6) 'Capt. Luce' in 1871 is matched to Grafton Luce on the roster's years only, no source gives his first name; (7) Purdy's amputation and the 1928 Gazette quotation are LighthouseFriends' account, not read in the original; (8) the Light-House Board's 1873 recommendation is quoted by LighthouseFriends only (the corpus Board volumes cover 1891 to 1901). OCR notes: the Herald OCR reads 'by Are' for 'by fire', so the Herald is quoted only for the date phrase. The Worcester Press appropriation list is OCR; the figure is read as $5000. The 1925 eclipse Bulletin is badly OCR'd; quotes are limited to the place names and the count. Checked on page images in the fact-check (2026-10-22): the 1925 Bulletin PDF p. 10 (printed p. 68) reads 'keepers of 19 lighthouses' with East Chop in the list of names (19 names counted); the 1922 Bulletin PDF p. 37 reads 'East Chop, Mass., oil to electric incandescent'. The nomination's purchase price for 1875 is OCR'd as '#5000' and is not used in the story. LighthouseFriends dates the automation to 1934 where the USLHS record gives 1933; the story states both. The Herald's fire notice reads 'by Are' in the OCR; the story quotes the Herald only for its date. The Worcester Spy names Silas Daggett as one of the Vineyard pilots, which the story uses.
